entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Al-ʻIjliyyah bint al-ʼIjliyyah was a 10th-century maker of astrolabes active in Aleppo, in what is now northern Syria.


She was born in the 9th century in the city of Aleppo, in the Abbasid Caliphate, and died in the 10th century, her work surviving as a testament to the ingenuity of medieval craftsmen.


Her astrolabes were used by scholars and astronomers to navigate the night sky and measure the positions of celestial bodies, contributing to a deeper understanding of astronomy and mathematics in the medieval period.


The legacy of Al-ʻIjliyyah's work can be seen in the continued use of astrolabes in ancient manuscripts and in the influence of Islamic astronomy on European scholars during the Renaissance.


A notable example of her craftsmanship is the astrolabe on display at the Topkapi Palace Museum in Istanbul, Turkey, a testament to her skill and artistry as a maker of precision instruments.


Al-ʻIjliyyah's story serves as a reminder of the often-overlooked contributions of women in the medieval period, and her work as a maker of astrolabes stands as a testament to the ingenuity and creativity of women in the face of cultural and social constraints.

entities.summary:
Al-ʻIjliyyah bint al-ʻIjliyy was a 10th-century maker of astrolabes active in Aleppo, in what is now northern Syria. 

  Born around 950 CE, she was a member of a family of craftsmen and learned the art of instrument-making from her father and grandfather. 

  Al-ʻIjliyyah's astrolabes were renowned for their accuracy and precision, and she became a leading figure in the field of astronomy in the Islamic Golden Age. 

  Her work not only contributed to the advancement of astronomical knowledge but also had a significant impact on the development of navigation and cartography. 

  Although the exact dates of her death are unknown, Al-ʻIjliyyah's legacy continued to inspire future generations of astronomers and instrument-makers. 

  As a testament to her skill and dedication, one of her astrolabes was discovered in the 19th century and is now housed in the British Museum, where it remains a fascinating relic of the medieval Islamic world.
